item.title: India's first Zika vaccine nears human trials after CDSCO panel review
item.description: An expert committee has recommended Phase I clinical trials for the vaccine developed by Indian Immunologicals and Australia's Griffith University, following a review of non-clinical studies ...
item.dc:creator: Sanket Koul
item.content:encoded: An expert committee of India's apex drug regulatory body, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), has recommended that government-affiliated drugmaker Indian Immunologicals Limited (IIL) be allowed to conduct Phase I clinical trials of the country's first vaccine for the Zika virus. The vaccine has been developed in partnership with Australia's Griffith University. Zika is a mosquito-borne infection primarily transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, with no vaccines currently available against the disease, according to UNICEF. The recommendation to proceed with trials was given to Human Biologicals Institute (HBI), the human health division of IIL, by the CDSCO's Subject Expert Committee (SEC) on vaccines, according to the panel's minutes of the meeting dated November 12, reviewed by Business Standard. The recommendation came nearly two months after HBI first submitted its Phase I clinical trial protocol to the panel in September this year. The protocol proposed a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety, reactogenicity and immunogenicity of a recombinant live attenuated Zika vaccine (freeze-dried) in healthy adult volunteers aged 18 to 50 years. At its September meeting, the committee had noted that while the firm had completed acute-dose and repeat-dose toxicity studies, along with animal immunogenicity and challenge studies, it had not submitted the scientific rationale for selecting the dose for the Phase I study. The panel had also sought statistical justification for the proposed sample size, the 3:1 randomisation ratio and the selection of cohorts based on non-clinical study findings. It added that HBI had submitted only a summary of the non-clinical studies rather than the complete study reports. “In view of the above and after detailed deliberation, the committee recommended that the firm should submit the above information for further deliberation,” the SEC had stated at its September 23 meeting. At its November meeting, the SEC reconsidered the proposal after HBI submitted the scientific rationale for dose selection and complete non-clinical study reports covering single-dose and repeat-dose toxicity, including immunogenicity studies. The recommendation comes two years after IIL signed a memorandum of agreement (MoA) with the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) to develop India's first recombinant live attenuated Zika vaccine. Under the agreement, ICMR will bear the costs of Phase I clinical trials, including expenses related to trial conduct, investigations and monitoring. The trials will be conducted at ICMR network sites across India. The SEC's recommendation is a regulatory step towards initiating human trials. The commencement of the study will depend on subsequent regulatory permission and trial-related arrangements. While Zika infection is typically mild and often does not require specific treatment, it can have severe consequences for pregnant women, potentially causing microcephaly and other congenital abnormalities in infants. In some cases, Zika infection may also result in Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a neurological disorder. India has experienced sporadic, localised outbreaks of Zika virus since its first confirmed cases in 2016. No confirmed cases of Zika-associated microcephaly or GBS have been reported in the country to date.

item.title: Motherson eyes bigger India play with global technologies to drive growth

Motherson eyes bigger India play with global technologies to drive growth The strategy is part of its broader Vision 2030 ambition to achieve USD 108 billion in topline gross revenue by 2029-30

Representative Image | Photo: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 12:31 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Auto components major Samvardhana Motherson International Ltd (SAMIL) aims to leverage technologies acquired through its global expansion to tap emerging opportunities in India's automotive market, as higher product standards and the shift to stricter emission norms drive demand for advanced solutions. The strategy is part of its broader Vision 2030 ambition to achieve USD 108 billion in topline gross revenue by 2029-30. In an interview with PTI, Pankaj Mital, Whole-time Director and President, and Gandharv Tongia, Group Chief Financial Officer, outlined the company's growth priorities, including bringing globally acquired technologies to India, expanding its presence across business segments and geographies, and strengthening its customer relationships.

"We believe that India's growth will also benefit us significantly, particularly because we now own many technologies. The quality of products being manufactured and consumed in India is improving, and the country is also moving towards the latest emission norms," Mital said. "With the acquisitions we have made, we have gained access to new technologies. We are delivering solutions that meet the standards of the best in the world, and these technologies are now part of our portfolio. We can therefore bring them to India and provide the best solutions to the market," he added. Also Read

Why Ola Electric is closing stores and turning to dealer-led retail network

Festive demand, export recovery drive auto sector growth, says MOFSL

2026 set for record auto sales, likely to touch 32 million units: Fada

Tata Motors plans local assembly of Iveco vehicles, eyes global expansion

Tata Motors PV sales rise 23% to 75,426 units in Oct on strong demand

On the domestic growth outlook, Tongia said India's automotive industry had maintained double-digit growth since the GST relaxation and the company expected the broader momentum to continue.

"India, as you know, the growth rate of our industry has been in double digits since the time the GST relaxation was done. By and large, we anticipate that the industry will continue to grow. It's possible that a quarter here and there might impact the performance, but structurally India is a consumption powerhouse and we anticipate that the growth level continues in India in times to come," Tongia said. He also said Motherson had a strong balance sheet and order book, supported by both organic and inorganic business additions, as it works towards its longer-term revenue ambition. "We are targeting a topline gross revenue of USD 108 billion in 2030. As mentioned, our balance sheet is very strong. We have a very strong order book organically as well as inorganically. We will continue to meet and exceed customer expectations and we are optimistic on our outlook," Tongia said.

Mital said the company's acquisition strategy would continue to be driven by customer requirements, with joint ventures and acquisitions considered when customers need solutions that the group cannot provide independently. "For us, the key consideration has always been what the customer wants. If our customers require solutions that we cannot provide on our own, we look at joint ventures or acquisitions to address those needs. Most of our acquisitions have been customer-led," he said. "Whether the requirement is in technology, in an area where we already operate, or in a completely new domain, you will not find us lacking in our efforts to find solutions for our customers," he added.

The group is also seeking to reduce its exposure to demand fluctuations in individual markets through diversification across automotive segments, geographies and newer verticals, while increasing its content per vehicle and adding new customers. "When we look at demand, we are well diversified and continue to add more segments to our portfolio. We have increased our content per vehicle. In the automotive segment, we have added new customers and expanded our presence in geographies where we were not present a year ago. We are also entering new verticals," Mital said. "Our 3CX10 strategy is always in play. That is how we plan for the group and focus on building diversification. If one segment is facing a downturn in a particular geography, we can still find solutions for ourselves in other segments or markets," he said.

On rising copper prices, Tongia said the company's wiring harness business, which accounts for around 30 per cent of group revenue, had contractual arrangements that allow changes in input costs to be passed on to customers at quarterly or six-monthly intervals. "Copper has risen sharply in recent times. In the wiring harness business, we have a contractual arrangement with our consumers, under which we can increase or decrease costs on a quarterly or six-monthly basis. So, to that extent, we don't expect any significant impact on our profitability because of copper prices," he said.

item.title: From bicycle parts to satellites: Inside Sunil Mittal's 50-year journey
item.description: As Bharti Enterprises marks 50 years, Sunil Mittal outlines plans to expand Airtel into AI, cloud, digital finance and satellite services ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / People / From bicycle parts to satellites: Inside Sunil Mittal's 50-year journey

From bicycle parts to satellites: Inside Sunil Mittal's 50-year journey As Bharti Enterprises marks 50 years, Sunil Mittal outlines plans to expand Airtel into AI, cloud, digital finance and satellite services

Bharti Enterprises chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal | Photo: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 12 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 12:26 PM IST

Listen to This Article

When Sunil Bharti Mittal set up a small manufacturing unit making bicycle parts in Ludhiana in 1976, he was barely 18. Fifty years later, the founder of Bharti Enterprises is presiding over a business empire whose flagship, Bharti Airtel, has become one of the world's largest telecommunications companies. The journey from bicycle crankshafts to mobile networks, submarine cables and satellite communications has been marked by bets that often ran ahead of the market, setbacks triggered by policy changes and three major crises that Mittal describes as Bharti's "Mahabharatas". Now, as the group marks its 50th anniversary, Mittal is preparing for another transformation. He wants Airtel to evolve from a telecommunications operator into a digitally enabled technology company, with connectivity at its core and businesses spanning artificial intelligence, sovereign cloud, digital finance and satellite services.

His prescription for India's digital economy is equally expansive: higher mobile tariffs, financially stronger telecom operators, a substantial expansion of network infrastructure and greater national control over strategic communications systems. The most immediate part of that agenda concerns what consumers pay for mobile services. Mittal believes average revenue per user, or ARPU, in India should rise to about ₹350 a month against the ₹300 benchmark he advocated roughly a decade ago. Rising operating costs and the investment needed to expand digital infrastructure justify the higher level, he said. Also Read

India must hold satellite 'kill switch', avoid reliance on one firm: Mittal

Sunil Bharti Mittal awarded France's Legion of Honour for business ties

Ahead of Starlink in queue for satcom nod, says Sunil Bharti Mittal

AI shouldn't be stifled, but unchecked use will be 'foolish': Sunil Mittal

France confers highest civilian honour on Bharti Enterprises' Sunil Mittal

"Everything is up. So, 350 would be the right ARPU for our industry," Mittal told PTI in an interview.

He compared the cost of mobile services with everyday purchases. "Now, you buy soap and a packet of chips. You know what it costs. Having a bottle of Pepsi costs you a lot more than that". At ₹10-12 a day, he argued, consumers receive access not only to calls and data but also to banking, education, healthcare records, direct benefit transfers, UPI payments and entertainment. "I think you can't say that is not affordable."   Airtel reported mobile ARPU of ₹271 in the September quarter, up from ₹256 a year earlier. Reaching Mittal's proposed level would require about a 29 per cent increase from the latest figure. The last major industry-wide tariff revision came in June 2024, when operators raised prices by around 10-25 per cent. Mittal did not give a timeline for reaching ₹350, saying, "I don't know".

FROM A BICYCLE CRANKSHAFT TO MOBILE PHONES Mittal's first venture was a modest manufacturing operation in Ludhiana, making bicycle components for the city's established bicycle industry. "I was only 18 at that time, and I started with manufacturing, not trading in bicycle parts, which, as you know, Ludhiana is pretty famous for," he recalled. "The dream is to sort of, you know, do something, create something for yourself, make your ends meet, and get enough fuel to fire your ambitions or dreams that one has at that time and age," he said. Bicycle parts were followed by hosiery and stainless steel sheets. Mittal then moved into importing and trading products that were relatively new to Indian consumers, including portable generators, push-button telephones, cordless phones, answering machines and fax machines.

"They were flying off the shelves. The margins were good," he said. But an early success also brought a lesson in the risks of doing business in India's tightly controlled economy. His portable generator business, which had become highly profitable, collapsed after the government changed its import policy. "Generator business, which was a very thriving, successful business for a few years, just went out overnight because the policy changed," he said. Having already built a business around telephone equipment, Mittal saw mobile services as the next step in communications. He had observed the development of cellular telephony in markets such as Britain and France and believed India would eventually embrace the technology, despite the high cost of handsets and services.

Bharti launched Airtel's mobile services in Delhi in 1995. The market was then in its infancy, with mobile phones largely beyond the reach of ordinary consumers. An agency survey had estimated that Delhi would have only 10,000 mobile subscribers in 10 years. "I knew that was not going to be the case," Mittal said. Airtel crossed that number within its first year. Even he had not anticipated how deeply mobile phones would transform everyday life. "Nobody could have imagined" that mobile telephony would become the "fabric of everybody's lives", he said. Airtel's early slogan was "Power to keep in touch". There was not even an SMS service at the time.

THE BET ON MARKETS RIVALS QUESTIONED One of the defining decisions in Airtel's expansion was its push beyond major cities into smaller towns and difficult markets, where demand was uncertain, and network deployment was more challenging. Mittal recalled that Hutchison's then chief executive, Hashim Ghosh, questioned the strategy. "You're making a big mistake going into these places. They will not have enough demand," Ghosh told him, according to Mittal. Airtel nevertheless pursued a pan-India presence, investing in markets including Bihar, Odisha, Assam and the northeast. In some of these regions, Mittal said, the company was, for some time, the only operator. "That's what I would say gave us the scale and the confidence to keep growing the business," he said.

The strategy was based on the expectation that falling tariffs and rising affordability would unlock demand well beyond affluent urban consumers. The subsequent expansion of mobile telephony across the country vindicated the decision and helped Airtel build a nationwide network. Another consequential decision concerned how the company would manage that network. When Airtel had around four to five million subscribers and wanted to expand to 25-35 million, it recognised that building all the necessary engineering, information technology and operational capabilities in-house would be difficult. Bharti vice-chairman Akhil Gupta proposed outsourcing network and IT operations to specialist vendors. The idea faced internal resistance, but Mittal backed it.

The model allowed Airtel to focus on customers, marketing and business strategy, while external partners took responsibility for much of the network equipment and its management. It drew surprise and criticism from international telecom peers before becoming a reference point for other operators. "It eventually became a Harvard case study, and a lot of companies followed that model later on," Mittal said. Bharti also invested ahead of demand in long-distance networks, enterprise connectivity and submarine cable infrastructure. Mittal described the Chennai-Singapore cable, built during the tenure of Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, as India's first such project. THREE MAJOR BATTLES AND THE JIO DISRUPTION The expansion was not without existential challenges. Mittal has identified 2002, 2009 and 2016 as three particularly difficult periods for Bharti, describing them as the company's "Mahabharatas".

The 2016 crisis coincided with Reliance Jio's entry into the market, when free introductory services and aggressive pricing triggered a price war and accelerated consolidation. Several operators exited or merged, while surviving companies faced pressure to invest in networks and retain customers. Mittal credits employees with helping Airtel withstand the disruption, recalling frontline teams engaging customers across states even as rivals offered free services. "In our case, our raw material was not the balance sheet. It was not the technology, because ultimately, it is the same technology. It was our people," he said. The upheaval left India with a far smaller number of major operators. Mittal believes the country should not return to the era when more than a dozen companies competed for subscribers. "India went too far into over a dozen operators," he said, arguing that fragmentation weakened balance sheets, divided spectrum and reduced the industry's capacity to invest. He considers three private operators, alongside state-owned BSNL, an appropriate structure for India. The comments come as Vodafone Idea continues to face financial challenges and BSNL works to rebuild its network and competitive position. Telecommunications, he said, is no longer simply a business of voice calls and data. UPI payments, banking, healthcare records, government benefit transfers, e-commerce, delivery platforms and streaming services all depend on reliable connectivity. Mittal also argued that existing networks have room to accommodate more customers and traffic. "All of us are running at 20, 30 per cent of our capacity of networks. So, we can take more traffic, we can take more customers," he said. TELCOS SEEK A BIGGER SHARE OF DIGITAL VALUE Mittal's call for stronger operators is linked to what he sees as an imbalance in the digital economy: telecom companies bear the cost of building spectrum, towers, fibre and network infrastructure, while online platforms often command much higher valuations. "We do all the hard work, but we don't get the same valuation and the profitability that those who don't make these investments get," he said. He cited the valuations of companies such as Google, Facebook and Netflix, as well as e-commerce, quick-commerce and streaming platforms that rely on telecom networks to reach customers. The issue reflects a longstanding tension in the global telecom industry, where operators make large, recurring capital investments while much of the commercial value generated by rising internet use is captured by digital services. Mittal welcomed Reliance Jio's recent listing, saying it would bring greater investor attention and research coverage to the sector. But he said the listing had no direct bearing on Airtel's valuation, which he described as already placing it among a relatively small group of global telecom companies valued above $100 billion. 5G'S REVENUE SHORTFALL AND THE NEXT TECHNOLOGY CYCLE Despite investment in next-generation networks, Mittal acknowledged that 5G has not delivered the new revenue streams operators had expected, particularly from industrial applications such as connected factories and automation. "That's been a disappointment globally," he said. The rollout has involved spectrum expenditure running into lakhs of crores of rupees across operators, with network deployment costs estimated by Mittal at another ₹1.5 lakh crore. He nevertheless sees the investment as necessary to support future demand. The next opportunity could emerge from 6G and what he described as "sensing networks", potentially taking shape over the next three to five years. In that environment, connected glasses, rings, watches and earpods could perform functions now handled by smartphones, and networks would increasingly interact with users' artificial intelligence agents. For Airtel, the ambition is to build businesses around growing demand for connectivity and computing rather than depend principally on mobile subscriptions and tariffs. Asked what the company might look like a decade from now, Mittal said: "It will be a digitally enabled technology company where connectivity will be at its core because everything will need connectivity". The vision includes digital financial services, sovereign cloud infrastructure, AI computing, fibre connections to homes and satellite links for remote areas. Mittal believes India has the potential to develop capabilities in artificial intelligence, large language models, quantum computing and space technology. But that will require a substantial expansion of physical infrastructure. India has around 350,000 mobile towers, compared to more than one million in China, he said, arguing that the country needs to double its tower base at least. More fibre, submarine cables, satellites and AI data centres will also be required. SATELLITES AND STRATEGIC AUTONOMY Satellite communications are another part of Mittal's strategy through Eutelsat OneWeb, in which Bharti has invested. The low-Earth-orbit network is intended to connect remote villages, forests, mountains, ships and aircraft where conventional mobile and fibre networks cannot economically reach. Mittal recalled persuading the British government to commit $500 million to the venture during the pandemic and said he subsequently invested $1 billion of his own money. He sees satellite services as complementary to terrestrial networks, rather than a substitute for them. "Where there is fibre, radio cannot compete with it. Where there is a radio, satellite cannot compete with it," he said. The commercial opportunity is only one part of the case. Mittal argues that satellite communications are increasingly important to national security, particularly as conflicts demonstrate the role of space-based connectivity in military operations. "The kill switch, as we call it, should not be sitting somewhere else. India must have control over its own space destiny," he said. He believes India needs multiple satellite providers, oversight of equipment and systems entering the country, and control over how data is routed. The position reflects growing concerns among governments about dependence on foreign-controlled communications infrastructure. Mittal said OneWeb services were functioning, with the company awaiting the final government signal to expand commercial operations. He cited the use of terminals for emergency services and recalled economic adviser Sanjeev Sanyal using one during a boat journey to Oman. THE BUSINESSES BHARTI LEFT BEHIND Mittal's career has also involved exits from businesses that did not become central to the group's strategy. Bharti entered modern retail through a partnership with Walmart and expanded into insurance through international partnerships, but eventually stepped back from those ventures. The Walmart venture faced resistance in India and did not develop as originally envisaged. "Walmart was literally blocked out of this country," Mittal said, adding that the American retailer later returned through its acquisition of Flipkart. Bharti also sold its general insurance business to ICICI Lombard and is bringing Prudential in as a partner in life insurance. Asked whether he regretted leaving businesses behind, Mittal said: "There are no regrets. We were too busy building our telecom story". The response reflects his emphasis on concentrating capital and management attention on businesses where the group believes it can build scale. Fifty years after starting with a single bicycle component, Mittal's ambitions now extend to the infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence, cloud computing and space-based communications. His central argument is that India's digital economy will require more investment in networks and stronger operators - even if that means consumers paying more for mobile services. The entrepreneur who once bet that mobile phones would find millions of customers beyond the major cities is now making a broader wager: that connectivity will remain the foundation of a much larger technology economy.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Guwahati-bound IndiGo flight returns to Pune due to technical issue
item.description: An IndiGo flight from Pune to Guwahati with 192 persons on board returned to Pune airport on Sunday after its landing gear failed to retract shortly after take-off, airport officials said. IndiGo ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Aviation / News / Guwahati-bound IndiGo flight returns to Pune due to technical issue

Guwahati-bound IndiGo flight returns to Pune due to technical issue IndiGo flight 6E 0623 (VT-IZE) reported a technical issue soon after taking off from Pune airport

Following the landing, the aircraft was escorted to Bay No. 7 by three fire-fighting vehicles and two ambulances as part of the prescribed emergency response procedures | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India Pune 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 12:06 PM IST

Listen to This Article

An IndiGo flight from Pune to Guwahati with 192 persons on board returned to Pune airport on Sunday after its landing gear failed to retract shortly after take-off, airport officials said. IndiGo flight 6E 0623 (VT-IZE) reported a technical issue soon after taking off from Pune airport. The pilot informed the Air Traffic Control (ATC) that the aircraft's landing gear (undercarriage) failed to retract and remained in the extended position, the Pune airport authorities said in a statement. Following the information, Pune airport authorities immediately coordinated with the ATC, IndiGo and other agencies concerned. The Indian Air Force (IAF), which manages the airport, declared a "full emergency", following which all prescribed emergency response procedures were activated, they said.   Fire services, ambulance services and other emergency response teams were placed on high alert to deal with any eventuality and ensure the safety of passengers and crew, the statement said. Also Read

Microsoft service disruption impacts IndiGo's email support services

IndiGo in talks with Brazilian planemaker Embraer to buy 100 jets

IndiGo, Asian Paints, IOC: Analyst view on crude sensitives as oil dips 13%

IndiGo CEO seeks lower Mumbai airport charges after Terminal 1 revamp

IndiGo to have 14 A321 XLR planes by end of 2027: CEO Willie Walsh

As part of the precautionary measures, the aircraft conducted a low pass over the runway to facilitate a visual assessment of its landing gear. After the assessment, the aircraft landed safely at Pune airport at 9.04 am, officials said. Following the landing, the aircraft was escorted to Bay No. 7 by three fire-fighting vehicles and two ambulances as part of the prescribed emergency response procedures. After confirming that the aircraft was in a safe and normal condition, the ATC withdrew the full emergency at 9.10 am, the officials said. Subsequently, the aerobridge was connected to the aircraft and all passengers were safely deboarded. "All 192 persons on board, including passengers and crew, were safe and no injuries were reported," the statement said. Meanwhile, IndiGo was arranging an alternate aircraft from Bengaluru to Pune to facilitate the onward journey of the affected passengers to Guwahati, it added.
